newsitem.title: USA: Oracle's Ellison to join Apple's board.
newsitem.headline: Oracle's Ellison to join Apple's board.

text.p: Larry Ellison, chairman of database software company Oracle Corp., is expected to join Apple Computer Inc.'s board of directors next week, a move which would push Apple to embrace low cost network computers.

According to industry sources, Ellison, who has long had an interest in buying Apple with his personal fortune, could announce his plans as early as Monday, just days before Apple unveils pieces of its strategy at a trade show in Boston.

Ellison would join Apple at a time when the computer maker is seeking a strategy to turn plummeting sales around. Since the board of directors ousted Gilbert Amelio as chairman and chief executive in early July, investors have been speculating that Apple's board may finally be prepared to radically change its strategy in an industry dominated by Microsoft Corp. .

Ellison revealed his appointment to the board of directors in an interview with the French financial newspaper La Tribune. He also told the newspaper he will invest his own money -- he declined to specify the sum -- in the company. His appointment will be announced on Monday.
Ellison could not be reached for comment. Apple and Oracle spokespersons declined to comment.
"Apple needs to and will exist because you need other players on the market," Ellison was quoted as saying. "You can't let Microsoft establish a monopoly."
On Nasdaq, Apple's stock jumped $1.688, or 9.6 percent, to $19.188, the highest price since January.

Ellison has been the computer industry's biggest cheerleader for the network computer, or NC, a low-cost device that draws much of its processing power from the Internet or a corporate computer network.
Because the NC would not rely on Microsoft's Windows software, it has won support from Microsoft rivals such as Sun Microsystems Inc. and International Business Machines Corp.
But none of the computer companies has devoted enough marketing resources to take on the juggernaut of the traditional personal computer industry.

For at least two years, Ellison -- estimated to have personal wealth of more than $6 billion -- has been interested in buying Apple with his own money. He has said he would use Apple's legendary brand to pitch the NC concept. But he has not made any serious attempt to buy Apple.

Ellison's appointment presumably would be backed by Steve Jobs, the Apple co-founder and adviser who is temporarily working full-time to set the company's strategy while a new chairman and CEO are found. Jobs and Ellison are personal friends.
Jobs, too, has said in a recent speech that the network computer is one of the best weapons Apple could use to fight back against Microsoft.
But it is unlikely that Apple would make the NC its core business and leave its Macintosh personal computer behind, analysts said.

"The NC would be fastest way for Apple to shrink from an $8 billion company to a $300 million company," said Kimball Brown, PC industry analyst at market researcher Dataquest. But by appointing Ellison to the board, Apple would gain credibility and strategic expertise, Brown said.
Still, Apple will likely have to change its business radically to survive, Wall Street analysts have said.
Ellison's appointment would come on the eve of the Macworld trade show in Boston, where Jobs is expected to unveil Apple's strategy for the next few months.
